questions.prompt: A patient with HIV asks whether Tamiflu would slow the release of new HIV particles, since HIV also buds out of cells. What is the best answer?

options.text: No — HIV leaves only by lysis, so a drug that targets budding has nothing to act on
Yes — Tamiflu also blocks reverse transcriptase, which HIV needs to bud out
No — Tamiflu blocks neuraminidase, which the course describes on influenza, not HIV
Yes — every budding virus uses neuraminidase to break free, so Tamiflu works on all of them

questions.explanation: Tamiflu is a neuraminidase inhibitor. The course names hemagglutinin and neuraminidase as influenza proteins; HIV buds without that target.

questions.prompt: A new drug blocks uncoating. Which viruses would it stop?

options.text: Only naked viruses, since an enveloped virus's genome is freed when the envelope fuses with the membrane
Only those entering by direct penetration, such as human enterovirus, since they release a capsid into the cell
Every virus equally, including bacteriophages, since every virus must uncoat in the same way
Those entering by membrane fusion or endocytosis (e.g., SARS-CoV-2, HIV, influenza), but not those entering by direct penetration (e.g., human enterovirus)

questions.explanation: Direct penetration pushes the genome straight in. Fusion and endocytosis deliver a capsid (or vesicle) that must be uncoated.

questions.prompt: SARS-CoV-2 deacidifies the lysosomes it travels through. What would you predict if a drug kept those lysosomes acidic?

options.text: The virus would switch to budding out through the plasma membrane, using neuraminidase to break free
Nothing would change, since lysosomes don't contain digestive enzymes and only act as transport bubbles
The acid would burst the host cell, releasing even more virions than exocytosis would
The lysosomes could digest the new virions instead of carrying them out, reducing the release of new viruses

questions.explanation: Lecture: lysosomes are de-acidified by the viruses 'and thus unable to digest them.' Keeping them acidic should restore digestion.

questions.prompt: Which step of the animal-virus life cycle has no counterpart in a bacteriophage infection?

options.text: Biosynthesis
Uncoating
Attachment
Release

questions.explanation: A phage injects only its genome; animal viruses that enter by fusion or endocytosis must uncoat the capsid to free the genome.

questions.prompt: According to the instructor's slides, why is HIV so hard for the body to clear once it becomes a provirus?

options.text: The viral DNA is built into the host's own DNA, where host defenses find it extremely hard to recognize and destroy
The provirus floats freely in the blood where antibodies can't reach it
The provirus is coated in chitin, which immune cells can't digest
The provirus makes thousands of new virions immediately, overwhelming the immune system

questions.explanation: Slides: 'It is incredibly difficult for host defense systems to recognize & destroy a provirus.'

questions.prompt: Host cells don't normally copy RNA into RNA. How does SARS-CoV-2 get its RNA genome copied?

options.text: Each virus brings a spare finished copy of its genome, so no copying is needed inside the cell
The host makes a viral enzyme (a polymerase/replicase) from the virus's own gene, and that enzyme copies the genome
Reverse transcriptase turns the RNA into DNA, which is built into the host chromosome as a provirus
The host's own DNA polymerase copies the RNA genome directly, using RNA nucleotides

questions.explanation: Lecture: the host transcribes and translates viral proteins, 'including an enzyme that makes copies of the viral genome.' Slides: replicases copy RNA.

questions.prompt: A budding virus is called a 'wolf in sheep's clothing.' Based on that idea, why would the immune system (and vaccines) target spike proteins rather than the envelope itself?

options.text: The envelope is made of chitin, which the immune system can't recognize or digest
Spike proteins sit inside the capsid, which is where antibodies collect after infection
The envelope is a patch of the host's own membrane; the viral proteins sticking out of it are the foreign part
The envelope is shed as soon as the virus leaves the cell, so only spikes are left exposed

questions.explanation: The envelope comes from the host cell membrane, so the virus looks like the host except for its viral proteins (Module 15: vaccines target the spike).

questions.prompt: During the 1918 flu pandemic, why were measures limited to things like mask mandates rather than antiviral drugs?

options.text: Tamiflu was available in 1918, but the strain's neuraminidase was a type the drug couldn't block
No one had ever seen a virus (that didn't happen until 1935), so its structure was unknown and no antivirals existed
Influenza was thought to be caused by a fungus at the time, so doctors relied on antifungal drugs
Antiviral drugs had already been developed, but they were banned for civilians during World War I

questions.explanation: Viruses were discovered in 1892 but not seen until Wendell Stanley used the electron microscope in 1935.

options.text: Enters by membrane fusion; leaves by budding
Enters by direct penetration; leaves by exocytosis
Enters by membrane fusion; leaves by exocytosis inside lysosomes
Enters by endocytosis; leaves by lysis

questions.explanation: HIV enters by membrane fusion (like SARS-CoV-2) and is seen budding out of CD4 helper T cells.

questions.prompt: A new drug blocks influenza's hemagglutinin. At which step would it act, and what would happen?

options.text: Attachment — the virus couldn't bind the host cell's receptors, so it couldn't enter
Biosynthesis — the host couldn't copy the segmented RNA genome
Uncoating — the capsid couldn't break apart inside the vesicle
Release — new virions would stay tethered to the host cell after budding

questions.explanation: Hemagglutinin is used for attachment; neuraminidase is used for release.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the SARS-CoV-2 infection cycle is FALSE?

options.text: New virions get their envelope as they bud through the plasma membrane.
New virions leave the cell by exocytosis as 'waste products.'
Its spike protein binds the ACE2 receptor on respiratory cells.
New virions are assembled with envelopes made from rough ER and Golgi membrane.
It enters by membrane fusion, releasing its single-stranded RNA genome.

questions.explanation: False — SARS-CoV-2 virions already have their envelope before release; they don't need to bud through the plasma membrane.

questions.prompt: Which statement about how viruses leave host cells is FALSE?

options.text: Exocytosis can be used by both naked and enveloped viruses.
When thousands of virions bud at once, the cell loses so much membrane that it is likely to die.
Budding always kills the host cell, even when only a few virions leave.
Enveloped viruses are typically released by budding.
Naked viruses are typically released by lysis.

questions.explanation: False — if only a couple of viruses bud out, the cell isn't harmed much.

questions.prompt: Which statement about retroviruses (instructor slides) is FALSE?

options.text: HIV is a retrovirus.
A retrovirus uses reverse transcriptase to turn its DNA genome into RNA.
The reverse-transcribed viral DNA is built into the host's DNA.
Retroviruses have RNA genomes.
A retrovirus built into the host's DNA is called a provirus.

questions.explanation: False — reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the RNA genome.

questions.prompt: Compare influenza and SARS-CoV-2 in four ways: how each enters the cell, where each gets its envelope, how each leaves, and which drug from the course works against each (and why not the other).
questions.explanation: Entry: influenza binds receptors with hemagglutinin and is taken in by endocytosis; SARS-CoV-2's spike binds ACE2 and enters by membrane fusion. Envelope: influenza takes a patch of plasma membrane as it buds out; SARS-CoV-2 is assembled inside with envelope from rough ER and Golgi membrane. Exit: influenza buds and needs neuraminidase to break free; SARS-CoV-2 travels in de-acidified lysosomes and leaves by exocytosis. Drugs: Tamiflu blocks neuraminidase, so it works on influenza but not SARS-CoV-2 (which doesn't bud); remdesivir disrupts the viral polymerase copying SARS-CoV-2's RNA genome, best taken early.

questions.prompt: Explain how a person can be HIV-positive for many years before developing AIDS. Use host range, membrane fusion, retrovirus, reverse transcriptase, provirus, and persistent infection in your answer.
questions.explanation: HIV has a narrow host range: its proteins bind CD4, found on human CD4+ helper T cells. It enters by membrane fusion. HIV is a retrovirus: its RNA genome is turned into DNA by reverse transcriptase, and that DNA is built into the host chromosome as a provirus, which is copied whenever the cell divides and is very hard for host defenses to recognize and destroy. This is a persistent infection: new viruses are made at a very slow rate — enough to be detected (HIV-positive) but not enough to cause disease. Months or many years later it may shift into a productive phase, producing lots of virus; that is when the person develops AIDS.
